H1.text: A bus brakes hard, and everyone lurches forward. It starts suddenly, and they fall back. A puck glides on and on across smooth ice.

H2.text: What links all three? One law, written by Newton.

H3.text: Aarav rides home with a water bottle in his front basket. At the college gate, he brakes hard.

H4.text: The bicycle stops. But the bottle flies forward, out of the basket. Nothing pushed it forward. So why did it move?

H5.text: Let's find out, with Newton's first law.

P2.text: Isaac Newton published it in sixteen eighty seven, building on Galileo's work.

P3.text: Every body stays at rest, or keeps moving at a constant speed in a straight line,

P4.text: unless an external force makes it change. In short: no net force, no change in velocity.

S1.text: Let's test it on the motion notebook. A two kilogram block slides off at four metres per second.

S2.text: On a rough floor, friction is strong. The block stops quickly. Its velocity line drops steeply.

S3.text: Make the floor smoother. Less friction, so the line drops more gently.

S5.text: Now turn friction all the way down to zero.

S6.text: The line goes flat. Four metres per second, and it stays four, for as long as we watch.

S7.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze, and draw every force.

S8.text: Weight pulls down. The floor pushes up just as hard. They cancel.

S9.text: With no friction, nothing is left over. The net force is zero, so the velocity never changes.

D1.text: Now the law in three small steps.

D2.text: Step one. Add up all the forces. The net force, sigma F, is zero.

D3.text: Step two. Zero net force means zero acceleration.

D4.text: Step three. So the velocity is constant. If it was zero, it stays zero. Rest is just a special case.

T1.text: Remember this. Zero net force means constant velocity, not always rest.

B1.text: Now, the bus. Link by link.

B2.text: The bus brakes. The brakes act on the bus, so the bus slows down.

B3.text: Friction from the floor slows your feet along with the bus.

B4.text: But nothing slows your upper body. By the first law, it keeps moving forward at the old speed.

B5.text: Feet slow down, body does not. So you lurch forward.

B6.text: When the bus starts, it is the other way round. Your feet move off with the bus, your body stays behind, and you fall back.

K3.text: Now you try. A bus takes a sharp left turn. Which way do standing passengers lean? Pause and decide.

K4.text: To the right! The bus turns left, but your body keeps going straight. So you lean outward, away from the turn.

V1.text: Side by side. A book resting on a table. Its weight and the table's push cancel. Velocity zero, and it stays zero.

V2.text: A car cruising at a steady speed on a straight road. The forward push and the drag cancel. Velocity constant.

V3.text: Your turn. The car moves at a steady sixty kilometres per hour. What is the net force on it? Pause and decide.

V4.text: Zero! Steady speed in a straight line means no acceleration. The forward push exactly balances friction and air drag.

W2.text: A twelve hundred kilogram car cruises at a steady twenty metres per second. Friction and air drag together are six hundred newtons. Find the driving force and the normal force.

W3.text: Constant velocity, so the net force is zero, both along the road and up and down.

W4.text: Along the road, the driving force equals the drag. Six hundred newtons, forward.

W5.text: Up and down, the normal force equals the weight. Twelve hundred times nine point eight. That is eleven thousand seven hundred and sixty newtons.

X2.text: Many students say: if the net force is zero, the body must be at rest.

X3.text: But zero net force means zero acceleration. The body can be at rest, or moving at a constant velocity, like the cruising car.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In concept questions on net force, and in finding a missing force when a body moves steadily.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A two kilogram particle moves at a constant velocity of three i plus four j metres per second. Two forces act: two i minus three j, and minus five i plus j newtons. What is the third force? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Three i plus two j newtons.

A2.text: Constant velocity means the net force is zero.

A3.text: Add the two known forces. Two minus five is minus three. Minus three plus one is minus two.

A4.text: The third force cancels them. Plus three i, plus two j. The mass and the velocity were not needed.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. Why does the bottle fly out of the basket when Aarav brakes?

Y3.text: Two. A car moves at a steady speed in a straight line. What is the net force on it?

Y4.text: Three. Why do you fall back when a bus starts suddenly?

N1.text: Next time: if zero net force means no change, how much change does a net force make? We find out in Newton's second law.
